playbook:
I track my actual budget from the stated starting figure at the top of the episode, minus everything I've actually won. This episode I stated 100 when my starting budget was 30 — a serious error. I read the starting budget carefully and never report a figure that doesn't match my real spend.

I recheck the starting budget at the very first decision and write it down; I never assume it from a previous game or guess it.

When a lot's standing high bid plus minimum raise is below my value in a non-final round, I bid the minimum raise — there are more rounds to react, so no reason to give up surplus early.

When the minimum raise equals or exceeds my value for the lot, I pass immediately, no matter how cheap the lot seems relative to estimate.

When I am already the standing high bidder in the final round, I always pass — raising only costs me against myself.

In the final round when I am NOT the high bidder, bidding the bare minimum is not enough: other bidders are also placing their last bids and can jump past me, as happened repeatedly (my 12 lost to 44, my 26 lost to 31). With no further round to respond, I bid aggressively — up to just below my full value (e.g., value minus the minimum raise or a shade less) — whenever the surplus at that price is still worthwhile. The final round is effectively a sealed bid: bid the most I'd actually be happy paying.

In the final round, I only walk away if the price I'd need to pay approaches my value and the remaining surplus is trivial.

When a lot is worth well above the current bid but bidding would consume most of my remaining budget and later lots remain, I check what later lots might be worth before committing; winning a near-zero-surplus lot early is almost never worth locking up budget.

I open cheap lots at the minimum rather than passing just to save budget — a small bid costs nothing and keeps me in contention.

I report the same budget number consistently within a lot and only decrement it when I actually win something.

Before bidding on any lot, I restate to myself: value to me, minimum winning bid, true budget left, round number, lots remaining. If it's the final round and the minimum bid is below my value, I bid near my value; otherwise I bid the minimum; if minimum bid ≥ value, pass.

A single plus-small-margin win (like my +12) can still leave points on the table by losing higher-value lots in final rounds — I'd rather win a 57-value lot at 50 for +7 than lose it entirely at 26.

1.text:
**Playbook for ref_auction**

- My budget number stays honest and simple: start at the stated budget, subtract any lots I've already won, and also subtract my current standing high bid if I'm the leader on the open lot. I never report a number above the original budget or one that contradicts my previous report. In the last episode I reported "106" — impossible nonsense that destroys credibility. I compute it once, carefully, and state the same figure consistently across rounds of the same lot unless I win something.

- My ceiling on any lot is my own value minus a real margin, never the estimate and never my full value. Profit = my value − what I pay, so on the final round I jump to just below my value (e.g., value 32 → bid 31; value 48 → bid 44-46). Bidding at or above my value turns a win into zero profit or a loss.

- A bid is only useful if it can win. With two rounds per lot, round 2 is effectively final: I never make a timid minimum raise there. If I want the lot, I bid to lead decisively at my value minus margin; if reaching the lead costs more than that, I pass immediately and stop reasoning.

- On round 1, a moderate bid (around 60–80% of my value, clearly above the minimum raise) stakes a claim. Round-1 bids don't need to be near my value — the real decision happens in round 2 — but token raises accomplish nothing.

- Rivals bid aggressively up to roughly the estimate and sometimes to exactly my value (lot 5: rival stood at 39, my exact value). So I expect the contest zone to reach the estimate; if my value is comfortably above the estimate I can win; if my value sits at or below the estimate, I expect to be outbid and shouldn't waste bids building hopeless positions.

- When the standing bid is at or above my value minus margin, I pass without hesitation. In the last episode I correctly passed on lots 2, 3, and 5 for exactly this reason; keep doing this instantly.

- Early on I got confused about my own budget. Budget only matters as a hard cap on what I can bid — I never bid more than I have — but my binding limit is almost always my value minus margin, which is usually far below the budget. I check the cap, then bid by value, not by budget.

- I play each lot on its own merits since future values are hidden: bid up to value minus margin on lots I want, pass on lots I don't. Don't hoard.

2.text:
My playbook for ref_auction:

- FIRST THING every turn: I re-read the stated starting budget and compute remaining budget as that number minus the sum of prices of lots I have actually won, and I report exactly that in [budget: N]. I never report money left from a previous turn's bid attempt, never invent a larger starting budget, and never copy a stale number from earlier in the episode. When uncertain, I recompute from the "results so far" list before writing the token.
- Before each decision I write in my reasoning: the stated starting budget, my value for the lot, the standing high bid, the minimum raise, my spend so far, and the resulting budget left. This checklist prevents both budget hallucination and unaffordable bids.
- My hard cap is my value; any bid above it is a guaranteed loss and I always pass there, no matter the round or how much I want the lot. If the standing bid already meets or exceeds my value, I pass immediately.
- On round 1 when the price is well below my value, I place the smallest raise that legally tops the standing bid. I do not jump early — early aggression just raises my eventual price.
- On the final round I weigh marginal surplus, not just "below value." Winning at value−1 gains almost nothing and locks up budget I may need for later lots with bigger gaps. I bid aggressively only when value minus bid leaves worthwhile surplus (several points, not one); if the best legal bid leaves near-zero surplus, I often pass and bank the budget.
- I never size deterrent bids by multiplying the standing price; I size by the gap to my value and the surplus I want locked in.
- I plan across lots: before bidding I consider whether later lots might offer better value-to-price gaps, and I avoid spending my last budget on thin-surplus lots early. A big win on an early lot that leaves me unable to afford a legal raise on a later cheap lot (as happened when I was stuck at 22 on lot 4) is a real cost.
- If the minimum legal bid exceeds my remaining budget, I pass — the bid would be invalid anyway.
- Each lot stands on its own profit math; I never chase a lot because rivals won earlier ones or because I have been winning.
- Unspent budget at the end is worthless, so on the final lots I spend down to the cap if positive surplus is available — but never below value.
- I keep reasoning to one or two sentences and always end with both bracketed tokens, [bid: N] or [bid: pass] and [budget: N], each on its own line, with the budget recomputed that turn.
